Article 32 guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Dr B.R. Ambedkar called it the “very soul of the Constitution and the very heart of it”, because rights without remedies are hollow promises.
— in S.P. Gupta (1981) the Court allowed public-spirited persons to approach it on behalf of those unable to do so; even letters were treated as writ petitions (Sunil Batra, 1980).
— compensation for violation of Article 21 was recognised in Rudul Sah (1983) and Nilabati Behera (1993); “continuing mandamus” let the Court supervise investigations (Vineet Narain, 1997).

— after Maneka Gandhi (1978) required procedure to be just, fair and reasonable, Article 21 grew to include privacy (Puttaswamy, 2017), a clean environment (M.C. Mehta) and speedy trial — all enforceable through Article 32.
— L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held judicial review under Articles 32 and 226 to be part of the basic structure.
Docket pressure, uneven access, and the risk of judicial overreach; the Court has at times asked petitioners to first approach High Courts under Article 226.

Article 32 has grown from a procedural guarantee into a dynamic instrument of constitutional justice. Strengthening High Courts and tribunals while preserving direct access will keep its promise meaningful.
